messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 46-year-old male

Admission date: [DATE]

Discharge date: [DATE]

Medical history: None reported except exertional dyspnea.

Chief complaint: Exertional dyspnea

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a chief complaint of exertional dyspnea. Physical examination revealed a systolic mitral murmur and a diastolic aortic murmur. TTE revealed a noncoronary SVA protruding into the mitral anterior leaflet, leading to moderate mitral regurgitation, severe aortic insufficiency, and a dilated aortic root. The ascending aorta measured 54-mm, and the left ventricular diastolic diameter was 75-mm, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 66%. No ventricular septal defect was detected. Coronary CTA showed no abnormalities or stenoses found in the coronary tree and the sac of the noncoronary SVA (measuring 36 × 47 × 51 mm) was protruding into the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. Surgery was performed via median sternotomy. The thickening of the wall of the tricuspid aortic valve and ascending aortic wall was consistent with inflammation. The patient underwent mitral valve and aortic valve replacement and replacement of the ascending aorta with an artificial vessel. Antibiotics were administered for 5 weeks. Follow-up TTE showed satisfactory functioning of both replaced valves. Aortic CTA demonstrated restoration of the normal anatomical relationship at the aortic root. The patient was discharged in stable condition.
Discharge diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge instructions: The patient was advised to follow-up with a primary care physician and cardiologist and adhere to medication and lifestyle modification recommendations.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The chief condition is a noncoronary sinus of Valsalva aneurysm protruding into the mitral leaflet and causing the aortic and mitral regurgitation that prompted admission. Its underlying cause is a congenital cardiac malformation, so it falls in chapter Q, congenital malformations. The closest category is Q24, other congenital malformations of the heart.

CODE: Q24
